title_en.text: Dalton Pass Memorial (Balete Pass National Shrine)

tagline.text: A national shrine on the mountain pass to the Cagayan Valley, site of a major World War II battle

location.label: Location
location.text: Santa Fe, Nueva Vizcaya (on the Nueva Ecija border, at the summit of Dalton Pass on the Maharlika Highway)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (as a stop within a Santa Fe trip)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (round-trip bus from Manila plus meals; entrance fee to be confirmed)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport, Manila (MNL), then overland

children.text: Dalton Pass is a zigzag mountain road linking Nueva Ecija and Nueva Vizcaya, about 910 m above sea level, where the Battle of Balete Pass was fought in 1945. The summit has a national shrine, memorials to Chinese and Japanese war dead and a viewing shelter, making it a worthwhile stop on the way to the Cagayan Valley.

Dalton Pass, also called Balete Pass, is a mountain road that joins Nueva Ecija and Nueva Vizcaya in central Luzon. It forms part of the Cagayan Valley Road section of the Pan-Philippine (Maharlika) Highway. According to Wikipedia, the summit lies at about 3,000 feet (roughly

) above sea level, where the Caraballo Sur and Sierra Madre ranges meet. As the gateway between Manila, the Cagayan Valley and the Ifugao rice terraces, it is crossed by almost every bus heading to northern Luzon. Santa Fe town is about
from Manila by road.

The pass has a history that reaches back to the late 19th century. Fr. Juan Villaverde, a Spanish Dominican missionary who worked in Nueva Vizcaya and Ifugao, is said to have proposed in an 1889 letter a route around the steep old trail, running along the slope of Mount Minuli. He judged its grade of about 5% suitable for carts and even a railway. Road construction began in the American colonial period and was completed in 1928. Because this road became the only land link between the Central Luzon plains and the Cagayan Valley, both armies had to control it in wartime.

The pass got its name from the Battle of Balete Pass in 1945. Part of the Battle of Luzon, it pitted the Japanese 10th Division against the US 25th Division. Wikipedia reports that the 25th Division suffered 685 killed and 2,090 wounded between February 21 and May 31, 1945, while Japanese losses are estimated at about 7,750. Filipino Commonwealth troops, Constabulary and guerrillas also lost 285 killed and 1,134 wounded, and eight Chinese militiamen fighting on the Allied side were killed. US Brig. Gen. James Dalton II was shot by a sniper on May 16, 1945 while surveying the battlefield, and on September 12 of that year Commonwealth Act No. 679 renamed the pass Dalton Pass. In the same period, at the nearby Villa Verde Trail (Salacsac Pass), the US 32nd Division suffered 825 killed and 2,160 wounded and Japanese losses are put at about 5,410, so the two battlefields together decided the course of the campaign in northern Luzon.

Today the summit holds the Balete Pass tourism complex. According to Wikipedia, it includes the National Shrine of the Battle of Balete Pass, memorials built by the Chinese and the Japanese to honor war victims, and, at the highest point, the "Dalton Pass Viewpoint with Shed" with wide views of mountains and forest. The site was declared a national shrine on May 10, 2016 under Republic Act No. 10796. It is not a large tourist attraction, but it is a meaningful stop on a northern Philippines trip where you can take in war history and mountain scenery at once.

Located at the highest point of the summit, the shrine was declared a national shrine in 2016. Its monuments and memorial facilities explain the course of the battle and show that this is a war site, not just a rest stop.

A marker installed by the National Historical Institute (NHI) in 2005 describes the Battle of Balete Pass of February–May 1945. It gives a short account of the fighting, so it is worth reading before you look at the monuments.

At the summit, a memorial to the Chinese militiamen who fought on the Philippine side stands alongside a Japanese memorial. What makes the site distinctive is that monuments remembering the dead of different nations are gathered in one place.
From the viewing shelter, a provincial project, you can look out over the ridges and forests of the Caraballo and Sierra Madre ranges. The view is best on a clear morning.

The road itself, with its continuous hairpin bends, is a sight. One travel writer says you can tell you have reached Santa Fe just from the way the vehicle sways from side to side. Since this stretch has frequent accidents, slow down if you are driving yourself.
A zipline, huts and basic facilities have reportedly been added for visitors in recent years. No official information on opening hours or prices is known, so check on site.

The area is known as habitat of Ceratocentron fesselii, a critically endangered orchid endemic to Nueva Ecija. It has orange flowers with a purple lip, but it is threatened by illegal collecting, so look but do not touch.

items.title: 1–2 hour stop
items.subtitle: A stop at the summit during a longer trip

children.text: If you are traveling north by private car, rental car or chartered van, park at the summit parking area. Whether regular long-distance buses stop at the summit is not confirmed, so ask in advance as described in the transport section below.
Read the historical marker and look around the national shrine monument. Knowing the battle dates and casualty figures beforehand makes the visit far more meaningful.
See the Chinese memorial and the Japanese memorial in turn, then look down at the mountain ridges from the viewing shelter.
If facilities such as the zipline are operating, try them and have a snack. Set off for your next destination before dark.
The view is probably best on a clear morning. On cloudy days visibility can be reduced.

items.title: Full day in Santa Fe
items.subtitle: Combining Dalton Pass and Imugan Falls

children.text: Arrive in Santa Fe town, have breakfast and find a tricycle.
Go to Imugan village and visit Imugan Falls. The round-trip trek takes about an hour.
Have lunch in Santa Fe town, then head to the summit of Dalton Pass.
Look around the shrine, monuments and viewpoint, and check the time of the last bus to Manila.
It is hard to see everything in one day by public transport alone. Hire a tricycle for the day or stay one night.
Take a bus bound for Isabela or Cagayan from a northern Manila terminal and get off at Santa Fe. One travel blog gave the fare as
and the travel time as
6–7 hours

, but this is old information from around 2020, so assume the current fare is higher and confirm it at the terminal. One source (undated) lists a Victory Liner air-conditioned bus from Manila to Santiago City, which passes through Santa Fe, at ₱594, so fares vary a lot by route and class. Travel time also varies with traffic.

The bus passes San Jose City in Nueva Ecija and Carranglan, then climbs the pass; just past the summit you are in Santa Fe. Ask the bus company and driver beforehand whether you can get off at the summit.

Santa Fe town is about 205–309 km from Manila by road (Wikipedia says 309 km, other map sources about 205 km, so the exact figure is not confirmed) and about 50–53 km from the provincial capital, Bayombong.
From Manila, take NLEX and SCTEX toward San Jose, Nueva Ecija; below the pass the Maharlika Highway continues.
The pass has constant sharp curves and steep grades, so use a low gear and do not overtake trucks recklessly.

items.title: Getting around from Santa Fe town

children.text: From Santa Fe town, hire a tricycle or local vehicle to reach the summit. Fares are negotiated, so agree on the round trip and waiting time before you go up.
The tricycle ride from the highway to Imugan village takes about
10 minutes
, and one blog gave the fare as
per person one way.
Santa Fe lies at about 913 m above sea level, so it is cooler than the lowlands. According to Wikipedia, average daily highs are
, lows are
, and annual rainfall is about 897 mm.

The November–May dry season is the most comfortable time to visit. Rain reduces visibility and makes the road slippery, so allow extra time in the wet season. May 10–13 each year is the Battle of Balete Pass commemoration period, set by a 1995 presidential proclamation; go then if you want to see the events, or avoid it if you prefer quiet. Event schedules can change from year to year, so check the latest announcements.

There is no confirmed information on lodging near the summit. To stay overnight, there are small lodgings in Santa Fe town or the provincial capital, Bayombong (about 53 km away). No specific business names or prices could be confirmed, so choose in person after you arrive.

Restaurants around the market in Santa Fe town are the most reliable choice for meals. Santa Fe is home to many Kalanguya (Ikalahan) people, and the town is known for handicrafts such as baskets and brooms. Santa Fe's town fiesta and the Kalanguya festival reportedly feature traditional games and food. The dates change each year.
The summit is about 910 m above sea level and can be cooler than the lowlands, so bring a light jacket and a raincoat.
If you are passing by bus, getting off at the summit may be difficult, so ask the driver in advance or use a tricycle from Santa Fe.
Remember that the monuments honor the war dead: keep your voice down and do not step on the stones.
Battle dates and casualty figures differ slightly between sources, so compare with the on-site signs as you read.
If you combine this with Imugan Falls on the same day, arrange the return ride (a tricycle that waits for you) beforehand.
Around May 10–13, parking and lodging can be crowded because of the events, so book ahead.
Avoid driving at night, and check the time of the last long-distance bus.
Dalton Pass is a dangerous stretch with steep grades and sharp curves where accidents are frequent, and the road has been blocked by the 1990 earthquake and by rainy-season landslides.
In 2017, 541 accidents were recorded on this pass, 21 of them fatal. On April 18, 2017, a bus fell off the road and dozens of people died.
The pass runs along the Digdig Fault, and during the 1990 Luzon earthquake 25 major landslides blocked the road. On heavy-rain days, check for landslides and road closures.
It has not been confirmed whether staff are on duty around the monuments at all times, so keep your belongings with you and do not stay alone late in the day.
A new bypass (the Dalton Pass East Alignment, about
23 km
long, with twin tunnels) is scheduled for construction in 2026–2031, so there may be traffic control around the work zones. Check the latest announcements.
A waterfall in Imugan village, Santa Fe. A tricycle ride of about
10 minutes
and a walk of about
30 minutes
get you there. It combines well with Dalton Pass in one day.
At Salacsac Pass in the Malico area of Santa Fe there is a shrine honoring the unknown soldiers who fought in the war. It is linked to the Battle of Villa Verde Trail.
UNESCO World Heritage rice terraces to the north in Ifugao. Dalton Pass is one of the gateways to them.
A quiet set of rice terraces in eastern Ifugao. It has fewer visitors than Banaue and is good for a relaxed visit.
